extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent applicants, attorneys, and agents
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining when prior art is disqualified under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) due to common ownership or obligation to assign, and the related examiner procedures, evidentiary standards, and form paragraphs for rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102/103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for common ownership at time invention was made
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement for common ownership at the time the claimed invention was made is intended to preclude obtaining ownership of subject matter after the claimed invention was made in order to disqualify that subject matter as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common ownership must exist at the time the claimed invention was made; ownership obtained after that time does not disqualify the subject matter as prior art. Determine common ownership based on the facts of the particular case.

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes common ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual ownership of the subject matter and the claimed invention by the same individual(s) or organization(s) or a legal obligation to assign both the subject matter and the claimed invention to the same individual(s) or organization(s) must be in existence at the time the claimed invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A moral or unenforceable obligation would not evidence common ownership. A license where basic ownership rights are retained by the owner does not defeat ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for establishing disqualification under 103(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of establishing that subject matter is disqualified as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) is intended to be placed and reside upon the person or persons urging that the subject matter is disqualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent applicants urging disqualification must establish common ownership at the time the claimed invention was made; patentees in litigation likewise bear the burden. Examiners or defendants should not be required to prove common ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant/representative statement as sufficient evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications and references will be considered by the examiner to be owned by, or subject to an obligation of assignment to, the same person, at the time the invention was made, if the applicant(s) or an attorney or agent of record makes a statement to the effect that the application and the reference were, at the time the invention was made, owned by, or subject to an obligation of assignment to, the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statement should be clear and conspicuous (e.g., on a separate piece of paper or in a separately labeled section) so the examiner notices it. Such a statement alone is sufficient evidence to disqualify a reference used under 35 U.S.C. 102(e),(f),(g) in a 103(a) rejection, absent material doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: When examiner may require objective evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: In rare instances, the examiner may have independent evidence that raises a material doubt as to the accuracy of applicant’s representation of either (1) the common ownership of, or (2) the existence of an obligation to commonly assign, the application being examined and the applied reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If material doubt exists, the examiner may explain the doubt and require objective evidence of common ownership as of the date of invention. Applicant may submit additional objective evidence (see next metric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evidence types to establish common ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence that may be submitted to establish common ownership includes recorded assignments, unrecorded assignment copies, affidavits/declarations by the common owner, or other evidence establishing common ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (A) reference to assignments recorded in the USPTO per 37 CFR Part 3 conveying entire rights to same person(s) or organization(s); (B) copies of unrecorded assignments filed in each application; (C) affidavit or declaration by an official of the common owner explaining facts supporting common ownership; (D) other evidence establishing common ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for disqualification of a reference under 35 U.S.C. 103(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: Such a commonly owned reference is only disqualified when (A) proper evidence is filed, (B) the reference only qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) or (g), or 35 U.S.C. 102(e) for applications filed on or after November 29, 1999 (i.e., not 102(a) or (b)), and (C) the reference was used in an obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All three conditions must be satisfied for the reference to be disqualified under 103(c). If the reference also qualifies under another subsection of 102 (e.g., 102(a)/(b)), it is not disqualified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement that present common ownership is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important to recognize just what constitutes sufficient evidence to establish common ownership at the time the invention was made. The common ownership must be shown to exist at the time the later invention was made. A statement of present common ownership is not sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Onda; evidence must relate to ownership as of the date the invention was made, not merely present-day ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedure when common ownership has not been established
rubrics_metrics.description: If the application file being examined does not establish that it and the reference patent(s) or application(s) are owned by, or subject to an obligation of assignment to, the same person, at the time the invention was made, the examiner will: (A) assume the application(s) and patent(s) are not commonly owned; (B) examine the application on all grounds other than any conflict arising from a possible 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 102(e),(f) and/or (g); (C) consider the applicability of any references under 35 U.S.C. 103 based on 35 U.S.C. 102(e),(f) and/or (g), including provisional rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103; and (D) apply the best references against the claimed invention by rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 until a statement of common ownership is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103 references against claims in applications filed on or after Nov. 29, 1999, the examiner should anticipate that a later statement of common ownership may disqualify a reference; follow MPEP procedures regarding finality of Office actions and subsequent statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedure when common ownership established (filed on/after Nov. 29, 1999)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the application being examined establishes that it and any reference patent or application were owned by, or subject to an obligation or assignment to, the same person, at the time the invention was made, the examiner will: (A) examine the applications as to all grounds except 35 U.S.C. 102(e),(f) and (g) as they apply through 35 U.S.C. 103, including provisional rejections under 102(e)/103; (B) examine the applications for double patenting, including statutory and nonstatutory double patenting, and make a provisional rejection if appropriate; and (C) invite the applicant to file a terminal disclaimer to overcome any provisional or actual nonstatutory double patenting rejection, if appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these steps for post-AIPA (after Nov. 29, 1999) filings where common ownership is established as of the invention date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedure when common ownership established (filed prior to Nov. 29, 1999)
rubrics_metrics.description: For applications filed prior to November 29, 1999, if common ownership at the time the invention was made is established, the examiner will: (A) examine the applications as to all grounds except 35 U.S.C. 102(f) and (g) as they apply through 35 U.S.C. 103; (B) examine for double patenting and make a provisional rejection if appropriate; (C) examine the later filed application under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as it applies through 103 and make a provisional rejection under 102(e)/103 in the later filed application, if appropriate; and (D) invite filing of terminal disclaimers and allow affidavits/declarations under specified CFR provisions where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different treatment applies pre-AIPA; examiners should follow MPEP § 706.02(l)(1) and related sections for applicable affidavit/terminal disclaimer options (37 CFR 1.130, 1.131, 1.132, 1.321).

rubrics_metrics.name: Double patenting rejections and terminal disclaimer remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonly owned applications of different inventive entities may be rejected on the ground of double patenting to prevent an organization from obtaining two or more patents with different expiration dates covering nearly identical subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double patenting rejections (statutory and nonstatutory) can be overcome in appropriate circumstances by disclaiming, pursuant to 37 CFR 1.321, the terminal portion of the term of the later patent and including a provision that the patent shall be enforceable only during the period commonly owned with the earlier application/patent. See MPEP § 804 and § 804.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples illustrating common ownership outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of examples illustrating when inventions are or are not commonly owned: Example 1: Parent owns 100% of Subsidiaries A and B — inventions of A and B are commonly owned by the Parent. Example 2: Parent owns 100% of Subsidiary A and 90% of Subsidiary B — inventions of A and B are not commonly owned by the Parent. Example 3: If same person owns subject matter and invention at time invention was made, license to another may be made without the subject matter becoming prior art. Example 4: Different Government inventors retaining certain rights (e.g., foreign filing rights) in separate inventions owned by Government precludes common ownership. Example 5: joint venture Company C facts — see text. Example 6: Company A owns 40% of invention #1 and 60% of invention #2, and Company B owns 60% of invention #1 and 40% of invention #2 at the time invention #2 was made — inventions #1 and #2 are commonly owned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the examples as illustrative guides to apply the factual test; outcomes depend on actual ownership/obligation to assign at the invention date.

rubrics_metrics.name: When an applicant's admission is not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. 103(c), an applicant’s admission that subject matter was developed prior to applicant’s invention would not make the subject matter prior art to applicant if the subject matter qualifies as prior art only under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) or 102(g), or, for applications filed on or after November 29, 1999, 35 U.S.C. 102(e), and if the subject matter and the claimed invention were commonly owned at the time the invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject matter and invention were not commonly owned, an admission that the subject matter is prior art would be usable under 35 U.S.C. 103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of when an invention is 'made' for purposes of common ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is 'made' when conception is complete as defined in Mergenthaler v. Scudder and In re Tansel; see Pfaff v. Wells Elecs. ('the invention must be ready for patenting...by proof that prior to the critical date the inventor had prepared drawing or other descriptions...sufficiently specific to enable a person skilled in the art to practice the invention').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common ownership at the time the invention was made must be determined with reference to conception/ready-for-patenting date, irrespective of whether the invention was made in the United States or abroad (subject to other statutes like 35 U.S.C. 104 for certain proceedings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of form paragraphs in making 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: The MPEP prescribes form paragraphs (¶ 7.20, 7.20.01, 7.20.02, 7.20.03, 7.21, 7.21.01, 7.21.02, 7.22, etc.) to be used when making 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejections and related provisional/common-ownership related statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraphs include statutory quotation, explanations, examiner notes and required follow-up paragraphs depending on filing date, type of prior art (102(e)/(f)/(g)), and whether common ownership is claimed. Examiners must follow the specified ordering and include Graham v. Deere explanations where required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional rejection based on copending application with common assignee or common inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: ¶ 7.21.01: Claim [1] provisionally rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being obvious over copending Application No. [2] which has a common [3] with the instant application. Based upon the earlier effective U.S. filing date, it would constitute prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) if published or patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provisional rejection may be overcome by (1) showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that the reference's undisclosed invention was derived from the inventor of the instant application; (2) showing a date of invention prior to the copending application's effective date under 37 CFR 1.131; or (for post-Nov. 29, 1999 filings) (3) showing common ownership at the time the invention was made. Use ¶ 7.15.01 if the claimed invention is fully disclosed in the copending application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham v. Deere factual inquiries for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co. that are applied for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) are summarized as follows: 1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art. 2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue. 3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art. 4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explanation applying the Graham v. Deere test must follow the form paragraph stating the rejection; use this test where appropriate in response to arguments invoking Graham.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 35 U.S.C.102(e) date rules (pre/post AIPA and international filings)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the rejection relies upon prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e), use 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as amended by the American Inventor’s Protection Act (AIPA) to determine the reference’s prior art date, unless the reference is a U.S. patent issued directly or indirectly from an international application which has an international filing date prior to November 29, 2000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply pre-AIPA or post-AIPA 102(e) date rules depending on whether the reference is a U.S. patent issued from an international application filed prior to Nov. 29, 2000 or other categories described in the Examiner Notes for form paragraphs 7.12, 7.12.01, etc.
